title: Incident triage and the attack story
subtitle: Turn related alerts into a defensible scope, priority, and response decision.
intro: A mailbox alert, an endpoint process, and a suspicious authentication can be successive steps of one intrusion. Investigating them independently can leave the attacker’s second foothold untouched. Defender correlates related signals into an incident so you can reconstruct a sequence, identify impacted assets, and record decisions in one place. SC-200 scenarios often give incomplete evidence and ask for the best next action: collect context, contain an active threat, or approve a verified remediation. Begin with the business impact and current attacker activity. Treat severity as a prioritization input, and treat every automated verdict as a conclusion that must be understood. Your objective is an evidenced attack narrative with verified containment and recovery.

sections.title: Build a sequence, not a list
sections.body: Read the incident summary and attack story, then open the underlying alerts. Establish the first observed event, the accounts and devices involved, and the relationships connecting them. A shared device, account, file, or campaign can explain correlation; temporal proximity alone does not establish causality. Follow the timeline through initial access, execution, credential theft, lateral movement, persistence, and any suspected exfiltration. A multi-domain attack may cross email, an endpoint, on-premises directory, and a cloud workload. Record what the evidence proves, what is only suspected, and which telemetry is missing.

sections.title: Prioritize and own the work
sections.body: Use asset importance, user privilege, evidence confidence, and whether activity continues to decide urgency. An apparently modest alert on a critical identity can deserve immediate attention. Assign an owner, start the appropriate workflow status, and record the next investigative action. In the legacy incident experience, status tracks work while classification records the investigation’s outcome. A true positive is a real threat; an expected authorized activity can be an informational/expected activity finding; a false positive means the detection incorrectly characterized the activity. Do not confuse severity, classification, and remediation status.

sections.title: Validate the outcome
sections.body: Inspect evidence verdicts alongside remediation states. Malicious evidence with a pending action is not fixed merely because the investigation finished. Review response history and correlate remediation with subsequent telemetry. Containment buys time; it does not remove persistence, restore stolen credentials, or establish that exfiltration never happened. Before closing, verify that affected entities were addressed, scope was expanded appropriately, and remaining tasks have owners. Microsoft’s incident-case experience is in preview as researched on October 15, 2026; a tenant may still show legacy incidents, so interpret the workflow described by the scenario.

remember: An alert is a detection signal; an incident organizes related attack activity.
Use raw alert evidence to verify the incident narrative.
A completed investigation and a completed remediation are different states.
Preserve scope, actions, rationale, and recovery evidence in the investigation record.
pitfalls: A high severity label does not replace business-impact assessment.
Closing an investigation record does not itself undo persistence or revoke access.
Product correlation is a starting hypothesis that analysts still verify.

lab.title: Reconstruct a simulated attack
steps: Use the official Defender pilot investigation walkthrough in a test tenant with supported licenses.
Open a sample or simulated incident and list the detected entities in chronological order.
Open two underlying alerts and document the actual events linking them.
Write a short triage note with urgency, owner, missing evidence, and the next containment decision.
lab.done: Your note links at least two telemetry sources and distinguishes verified actions from recommended actions.

questions.stem: An incident contains a phishing alert, a script execution alert, and an authentication alert on a file server. The endpoint is still making suspicious connections. Which action best advances the investigation while addressing immediate risk?
options: Resolve the phishing alert because the message was deleted, then close the incident.
Export only the first alert and investigate all remaining alerts as unrelated events.
Assess the connected evidence and affected assets, contain the active foothold, and continue scoping.
Lower incident severity until every individual alert has a final verdict.
explanations: Message removal leaves endpoint execution and lateral access unexplained.
This discards the relationships needed to understand the attack.
Correct. Correlation guides scope while ongoing activity justifies timely containment.
Incomplete scope is not a reason to delay containment or lower priority.
questions.takeaway: Prioritize the active attack and investigate its linked stages.

questions.stem: A SOC is handing an active incident to the next shift. Which TWO details most directly support accountable follow-up?
options: A record of affected assets and response actions with their current states.
An assigned owner and documented next investigative action.
A lower severity chosen to keep the incident out of the urgent queue.
A false-positive classification solely because a malicious file was quarantined.
explanations: Correct. The next analyst needs scope and actual response state.
Correct. Ownership and next steps prevent lost work.
Queue appearance is not an evidence-based severity criterion.
A successfully remediated real threat remains a true positive.
questions.takeaway: Handoffs need ownership, scope, action state, and rationale.

questions.stem: Automated analysis marks an email cluster malicious. A related device action is pending approval. The incident has no recent alerts. What conclusion is justified?
options: The response remains incomplete until pending actions are evaluated and outcomes verified.
The incident must be false positive because it is now quiet.
A malicious verdict means every remediation already ran successfully.
The absence of new alerts proves the attack has been eradicated.
explanations: Correct. Verdict, action status, and verification answer different questions.
A quiet environment does not invalidate malicious evidence.
Verdicts do not imply action execution.
Silence can reflect inactivity, missing telemetry, or effective containment.
questions.takeaway: Always separate evidence verdicts from response execution.

questions.stem: A scheduled, approved security exercise correctly triggers a suspicious activity detection. After verifying the authorization and matching events, how should the analyst reason about classification?
options: Classify it as malicious solely because the detector fired.
Mark it false positive without checking whether the detector correctly identified the behavior.
Use the expected/authorized-activity outcome supported by the portal and document the exercise.
Leave it active indefinitely to avoid recording a determination.
explanations: Detection of behavior is not proof of unauthorized intent.
A detector can be correct about behavior while the activity is expected.
Correct. Correctly detected authorized behavior differs from a detection error.
Verified findings should be documented and the workflow completed.
questions.takeaway: Classify the observed activity and its authorization accurately.

questions.stem: Which immediate endpoint action best matches the stated containment requirement?
options: Offboard the workstation from Defender.
Isolate the onboarded device using the supported Defender action.
Close the alert so the script stops.
Delete all timeline records before investigating.
explanations: Offboarding removes the monitoring relationship and does not provide the requested supported containment.
Device isolation restricts network communication while preserving the supported Defender connection.
Changing an alert status is not an endpoint containment action.
Removing evidence would neither meet the containment requirement nor preserve investigation context.
questions.context:
CASE 2 — NORTHSTAR LABS

The CFO reports a suspicious message. Defender for Office 365 shows it was delivered, and investigators have its NetworkMessageId and the recipient address. EmailUrlInfo contains a suspicious domain; there is not yet verified click evidence.

Minutes later the CFO’s onboarded workstation starts an unusual script and continues making suspicious outbound connections while files are being modified. Entra sign-in evidence also supports theft of an authenticated cloud session. There are other recipients of related messages, but the full scope is unknown.

Northstar requires supported containment that preserves the endpoint’s Defender service connection. The analyst must investigate message recipients, endpoint execution, and identity access as connected workstreams. An incident is not considered resolved until the team verifies response actions, checks for persistence, and documents scope and residual risk. Assume the relevant services are deployed and the analyst has the required permissions.
questions.takeaway: Device isolation restricts network communication while preserving the supported Defender connection.

questions.stem: Which TWO investigative conclusions are justified by the case evidence?
options: A URL in EmailUrlInfo proves the CFO clicked it successfully.
Investigate Safe Links click telemetry and endpoint connection evidence to test the click hypothesis.
Scope the related message recipients and inspect the compromised identity’s session and persistence activity.
A delivered email proves every recipient’s device is compromised.
explanations: URL presence establishes content, not user interaction or successful navigation.
These sources can test the unproven user-click and device-contact portions of the chain.
The evidence spans email, endpoint, and identity; scope and persistence require investigation across them.
Delivery alone does not establish execution or compromise for every recipient.

questions.stem: The workstation is isolated and malicious messages have been removed. Evidence still supports a stolen cloud session. What response remains necessary?
options: Declare recovery because device isolation stops all cloud access.
Address identity access and sessions, then verify the resulting containment and persistence state.
Only lower the incident severity.
Assume deleting email automatically invalidates every authentication token.
explanations: Endpoint isolation is not equivalent to revoking an attacker’s cloud session.
Identity containment and validation are still required for the separately evidenced access path.
Severity is a triage attribute, not account remediation.

questions.stem: After urgent containment, arrange Northstar’s evidence-based path to closing the incident.
options: Document disposition, completed actions, remaining risk, and accountable follow-up before closure.
Investigate the affected entities and establish scope and persistence.
Verify that executed response actions succeeded and validate recovery.
Remediate the validated persistence and affected access paths through the appropriate products.
explanations: Closure follows a documented explanation of what was done and what remains.
Establish the actual attack scope and persistence before selecting full remediation.
Success must be checked rather than inferred from a submitted action.

title: Endpoint timelines, files, and entity evidence
subtitle: Follow process relationships and artifacts to establish what ran and where else it appeared.
intro: A suspicious executable name is only a clue. The same name can identify unrelated files, and legitimate administration tools can be abused. A useful endpoint investigation connects a process to its parent, command line, account, file identity, network activity, and neighboring events. The device timeline gives local sequence; file and URL entity pages provide organizational context. SC-200 tests the ability to choose the next pivot that answers a specific question, rather than selecting every available tool. Work from known identifiers and a narrow time range, then expand when the evidence supports it. Capture relevant findings before retention windows or remediation remove details that you may need to explain the incident.

sections.title: Read the device timeline
sections.body: Open the device from the alert or incident and inspect events around the suspicious activity. Select process events to review parent-child relationships, executable paths, command lines, and the account context. Compare execution with file creation, persistence changes, and outbound connections. Timeline filters help focus an investigation, but an overly narrow range can hide the initial download or later lateral movement. A device profile’s Last seen value can lag other evidence; an older label alone does not prove that a device stopped sending useful telemetry. Flag relevant events and retain the identifiers required for later hunting.

sections.title: Use entity-specific pivots
sections.body: A file page can show hashes, signatures, prevalence, observed devices, associated alerts, and file names. Low prevalence increases investigative interest but is not a malicious verdict. A valid signature also does not establish authorized use. Use the stable file hash to investigate the same artifact across devices, then examine execution context on each affected host. URL and domain pages connect network observations with email and click activity. A domain seen in a message and on a device can support a phishing-to-execution hypothesis, but verify timestamps and process associations before drawing that conclusion.

sections.title: Explain the chain and its limits
sections.body: An incident graph helps relate artifacts to alerts, while the timeline and raw events support the sequence. For a suspected lateral move, identify the source identity, originating host, destination host, and remote activity; do not assume a shared account proves an intrusion. Different views and tables can have different lookback periods, and tenant retention settings matter. When required evidence is missing, distinguish “not observed” from “did not occur.” Export or otherwise preserve the relevant evidence under your organization’s process, then record a concise narrative that another analyst can reproduce using the same IDs and times.

remember: Use file hashes, device IDs, account IDs, and timestamps to make pivots repeatable.
Process ancestry and command lines explain execution context.
File prevalence and a signature are supporting evidence, not proof of safety.
A domain page can connect endpoint, message, and click observations.
pitfalls: A file name is not a unique artifact identifier.
A timeline filter can conceal the event that explains the alert.
A graph edge represents a relationship, not automatic proof of causation.

lab.title: Trace an endpoint artifact
steps: Open a benign simulated endpoint alert in a test environment.
Review the parent process, child process, command line, account, and nearby network events.
Pivot to the file page by hash and list other devices where it was observed.
Open a related domain page if available and compare timestamps across its device and email observations.
lab.done: You can explain a reproducible sequence and identify which observations still require validation.

sources.title: Endpoint alert evidence and process context

questions.stem: An alert shows powershell.exe starting immediately after an Office application. You need to determine whether the script came from the document or from routine management. What is the best first pivot?
options: Block every file with the name powershell.exe.
Assume the Microsoft signature proves the execution is safe.
Use only the device’s vulnerability recommendations to classify execution.
Inspect the process tree, command line, account, and neighboring timeline events.
explanations: Name-based blanket blocking is not an investigation of this event.
Signed binaries can run attacker-controlled commands.
Posture recommendations do not reconstruct this process chain.
Correct. Execution context can distinguish an Office-launched payload from authorized management.
questions.takeaway: Process context matters more than a familiar executable name.

questions.stem: A newly discovered file may have spread to several devices. Which TWO actions most directly establish artifact scope?
options: Inspect execution and related alerts on the devices where that hash appeared.
Declare the file safe because it has low organizational prevalence.
Use the file hash to open its entity profile and review observed devices.
Treat identical file names on different hosts as cryptographic matches.
explanations: Correct. Presence and execution impact need device context.
Low prevalence does not establish safety.
Correct. Hash identity supports a consistent artifact pivot.
Names can identify different content.
questions.takeaway: Track the same artifact, then validate its behavior on each host.

questions.stem: A domain appears in a phishing message and in a device timeline. The analyst wants to determine whether the recipient clicked it and which device contacted it. Which view best supports this correlation?
options: The email’s display sender name without any other evidence.
The file vulnerability list alone.
The device security-policy tab alone.
The domain/URL entity page, followed by its email, clicks, and associated device views.
explanations: Display names are weak identifiers and contain no contact timeline.
Software weaknesses do not answer this correlation question.
Policy state does not establish message click or network contact.
Correct. This entity page exposes the relevant cross-workload observations.
questions.takeaway: Use the entity page that spans the observations you need.

questions.stem: A device’s Last seen summary predates a recent suspicious event present in its timeline. What should the investigator do?
options: Discard the timeline event because the summary timestamp always overrides it.
Close the incident because the device cannot have produced newer data.
Reinstall the sensor immediately without checking the event details.
Investigate the actual timeline event and verify telemetry health before declaring the device offline.
explanations: The summary is not authoritative for every evidence type.
The newer observed event requires investigation.
Reinstallation does not explain the event and may disrupt evidence collection.
Correct. Microsoft documents that profile Last seen may omit some evidence.
questions.takeaway: Validate detailed evidence instead of overinterpreting a summary field.

title: Endpoint containment and live response
subtitle: Choose the action that meets the containment or evidence requirement and verify its result.
intro: An analyst must distinguish preserving evidence, containing communication, and removing a threat. Isolating a device limits network access; collecting an investigation package captures diagnostic artifacts; live response enables an authorized remote investigation. These are complementary actions with different impact and prerequisites. SC-200 questions often specify an urgent operational constraint, such as continuing Defender connectivity or collecting forensic context without running an arbitrary script. Match that constraint to the action and check the action’s actual state. Availability depends on platform, device onboarding, license, permissions, and sometimes selective response restrictions. After an automatic action, investigate why it occurred before releasing the asset. A green completed status describes an action, not necessarily a fully recovered incident.

sections.title: Match actions to the objective
sections.body: Use device isolation when you must reduce communication with the environment while retaining the required Defender service connection. Application restrictions are different: restricting application execution allows Microsoft-signed applications and is not a network quarantine. An antivirus scan seeks threats; an investigation package gathers device-state artifacts for analysis. Do not replace evidence collection with deletion simply because a file looks suspicious. Record why an action is justified and consider critical-service impact. An unavailable action can reflect OS support, onboarding, RBAC scope, or high-value-device selective permissions; it does not automatically mean the portal is broken.

sections.title: Use live response deliberately
sections.body: Live response provides a remote shell for deeper investigation and supported remediation. Basic and advanced permissions differ, and commands have platform-specific support. Review the command log and prefer the least disruptive commands that answer the question. For example, inspect process or persistence information, collect an artifact, and only then run an authorized remediation when necessary. Scripts run through the approved library mechanism; uploading an unreviewed arbitrary command is not a substitute for an evidence plan. End the session when finished, preserve outputs, and review action history to confirm what actually ran.

sections.title: Understand automatic actions and current changes
sections.body: Attack disruption can apply containment automatically; the incident and Action center explain the affected assets and actions. Review the current enforced state rather than assuming a historical completed entry means a policy is still active. Release assets only after checking scope, removing the cause, and mitigating risk. As of September 1, 2026, Microsoft states that Defender for Endpoint AIR no longer runs as a separate, manually triggerable investigation experience: its protection capabilities run in the default antivirus stack, with a full antivirus scan available on demand. This change is specific to Endpoint; Defender for Office 365 AIR continues.

remember: Isolation retains required Defender connectivity; it is not shutdown.
Investigation packages collect artifacts; scans seek and remediate threats.
Live response requires supported platform, permissions, and a connected onboarded device.
MDE’s separate manually triggered AIR experience changed on September 1, 2026.
pitfalls: Contain user at endpoint level is different from disabling a directory account.
A completed containment event does not prove containment remains enforced today.
Old device-menu documentation can still show retired AIR workflow labels.

lab.title: Practice response without production impact
steps: Use an onboarded lab endpoint and verify your role and live-response settings.
Collect an investigation package and locate the completed action/download.
Start live response, run supported read-only commands such as help and processes, and review the command log.
In a planned maintenance window, isolate the lab endpoint, verify Defender access, then release it and confirm the result.
lab.done: You can show evidence collection, the live-response audit trail, and successful isolation/release status.

questions.stem: Ransomware activity continues on an onboarded workstation. You must reduce network communication while keeping the device connected to Defender for investigation. Which action best matches the requirement?
options: Restrict app execution only.
Collect investigation package only.
Isolate device.
Remove the device from Defender onboarding.
explanations: Application restrictions do not provide the requested network boundary.
Collection captures evidence but does not contain communication.
Correct. Isolation limits network traffic while preserving required Defender service communication.
Offboarding removes useful management and visibility rather than providing response isolation.
questions.takeaway: Use isolation for network containment with Defender connectivity.

questions.stem: A junior analyst needs to collect context from a live-response session without deleting evidence. Which TWO practices are appropriate?
options: Check whether the assigned role permits the necessary basic or advanced commands.
Use supported read-only commands and preserve their outputs and command log.
Run remediate against every unfamiliar process before collecting context.
Assume every Windows command works identically on Linux and macOS.
explanations: Correct. Command access and platform support constrain the session.
Correct. Read-only investigation preserves useful state.
Unfamiliar does not mean malicious, and deletion can remove evidence.
Live-response command support varies by platform.
questions.takeaway: Plan live-response collection around authorization and platform support.

questions.stem: An automatic disruption contains a device. The attack has stopped visibly, but recovery is not yet verified. Arrange the appropriate response workflow.
options: Verify remediation and assess residual risk before authorizing release.
Release the contained asset and verify normal, safe operation.
Remove persistence and mitigate the identified cause.
Inspect the attack story, current containment state, and affected scope.
explanations: This verification gate belongs after remediation and before release.
Release comes after risk mitigation and verification.
Remediation follows investigation of scope and cause.
First understand why containment happened and what is affected.
questions.takeaway: Containment release is a recovery decision that follows evidence and mitigation.

questions.stem: It is October 2026. An analyst wants an on-demand endpoint investigation and follows an old guide that says to manually initiate MDE AIR. What is the current documented approach?
options: Offboard and re-onboard the device to make the old manual button appear.
Use a full antivirus scan as needed and investigate through current endpoint evidence and response tools.
Assume all antivirus response capabilities were removed with the separate AIR experience.
Enable Office 365 AIR to recreate the retired MDE investigation experience.
explanations: Changing onboarding does not restore a retired experience.
Correct. Microsoft’s September 2026 change retains automatic protection and recommends a full scan on demand.
Protection continues in the default antivirus stack.
MDO AIR addresses email and remains a separate workload.
questions.takeaway: Follow the dated Endpoint change notice; distinguish MDE from MDO AIR.

title: Email and collaboration investigation
subtitle: Trace delivered messages, authentication, URLs, and recipients before selecting remediation.
intro: A message can pass delivery checks and become malicious later, or it can be delivered because an override altered normal protection. A useful investigation therefore asks what the message contained, which controls evaluated it, where it went, whether anyone interacted, and what changed afterward. Threat Explorer, the email entity page, and URL pivots help answer these questions. SC-200 expects you to interpret evidence under licensing and permission constraints. Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 provides Real-time detections, while Plan 2 provides Threat Explorer with broader hunting and response capabilities. Do not infer that every recipient was compromised because one copy was malicious; investigate interaction and account activity separately.

sections.title: Find and scope the message
sections.body: Start with strong identifiers such as network message ID, sender, recipient, URL, attachment hash, and a narrow delivery interval. Threat Explorer’s All email view can include benign and malicious inbound, outbound, and internal mail. Broaden carefully from the seed message to related recipients, shared URLs, or campaign evidence. Subject alone is a weak campaign key because attackers reuse common subjects and legitimate messages may match. URL click information helps prioritize potentially exposed users, but a recorded click still needs context such as blocking, click verdict, device evidence, and subsequent authentication activity.

sections.title: Explain delivery and later state
sections.body: The email entity page brings together delivery details, headers, authentication results, attachments, URLs, and related messages. Compare original delivery with latest delivery location and post-delivery actions. Latest location reflects system and administrator actions; it does not guarantee the message’s live folder after all user moves. Inspect SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication as evidence about sender authentication, not as a universal safety certificate. A compromised legitimate sender can authenticate successfully. Check overrides when an unexpected message was delivered or blocked, and identify which policy or allow entry influenced that decision.

sections.title: Follow compromise beyond email
sections.body: A clicked link may lead to credential theft, OAuth consent, script execution, or financial fraud without a malware attachment. Pivot from the message to URL, account, and device evidence to test those hypotheses. Review timeline ordering so you do not mistake unrelated activity for progression. Previewing or downloading message content requires appropriate permissions beyond reading metadata. After confirming malicious delivery, define the exact message set for remediation, preserve relevant evidence, and address compromised accounts separately. If no user interaction or downstream activity is observed, document that visibility limit rather than claiming that compromise was impossible.

remember: Plan 1 Real-time detections and Plan 2 Threat Explorer have different capabilities.
NetworkMessageId supports precise message pivots.
Original delivery and latest observed delivery location answer different questions.
Successful authentication does not guarantee benign content or intent.
pitfalls: Do not select a mass-remediation set by subject alone.
A click is evidence of interaction, not an automatic account-compromise verdict.
Metadata visibility does not automatically grant email-content access.

lab.title: Investigate a benign test message
steps: Send a clearly labeled harmless test email between lab mailboxes.
Find the message in the available investigation experience and record network message ID and recipients.
Open its email entity page; compare authentication, delivery, URL, and attachment details.
Read the documented override examples and explain how you would investigate an unexpected allow decision.
lab.done: You can identify the exact message and explain delivery evidence without equating authentication with safety.

Threat Explorer, using strong message and entity filters.
