questions.stem: A message is suspected phishing even though SPF, DKIM, and DMARC passed. Which TWO follow-up checks are most useful?
options: Treat passing authentication as a definitive clean verdict.
Investigate whether the legitimate sender or recipient account shows compromise-related activity.
Inspect URL, attachment, header, and threat evidence on the email entity page.
Ignore click evidence because authenticated mail cannot contain phishing URLs.
explanations: Authentication validates aspects of sender identity, not benign intent.
Correct. Legitimate infrastructure can be abused after account compromise.
Correct. Content and delivery evidence remain relevant.
Authenticated mail can still carry attacker-controlled links.
questions.takeaway: Authentication and maliciousness are separate assessments.

questions.stem: An email’s latest delivery location shows Inbox. A user says they later archived it. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: The field reflects observed system/admin delivery changes and does not guarantee the current folder after user actions.
The message was never delivered because archive actions erase delivery history.
The user must be wrong because the field is a live mailbox-folder lookup.
The message is benign because it is no longer in the inbox.
explanations: Correct. Microsoft explicitly documents this latest-location limitation.
Archiving does not invalidate original delivery evidence.
User moves are not fully represented by this field.
Folder location does not establish message safety.
questions.takeaway: Read delivery fields according to their documented semantics.

questions.stem: A phishing message was delivered unexpectedly. The analyst has confirmed the exact message and wants to explain which exception changed filtering. What should be reviewed next?
options: The endpoint device-group automation level as the email-delivery authority.
Only the display name in the From field.
The override details and the corresponding policy or allow entry.
Every message with the same subject, with immediate hard deletion.
explanations: Endpoint automation levels do not govern email filtering overrides.
Display name alone cannot explain policy processing.
Correct. Override evidence can explain an unexpected filtering outcome.
This neither explains delivery nor safely scopes remediation.
questions.takeaway: Investigate the policy decision that affected the exact message.

title: Email remediation, AIR, and attack disruption
subtitle: Remove the correct message set, approve or automate actions, and verify account recovery.
intro: Finding a malicious message is only the start of email response. You must remove the appropriate copies, check whether the sender or recipient account is compromised, and verify what automated protection already did. Microsoft provides multiple mechanisms with distinct purposes: Zero-hour auto purge revisits delivered threats, Office 365 AIR expands an investigation and proposes remediation, and XDR attack disruption contains active attacks across compromised assets. Manual Threat Explorer actions provide a scoped response when an analyst has enough evidence. SC-200 questions reward recognizing which mechanism already ran, whether an approval remains pending, and which additional action addresses the actual risk. Keep evidence, action state, and account recovery separate in your reasoning.

sections.title: Choose a scoped removal workflow
sections.body: In Threat Explorer, select the verified message set and use Take action. Moving mail to Deleted Items differs from soft deletion into Recoverable Items; hard deletion has different recovery implications and still must respect retention and preservation requirements. A two-person process can use Propose remediation to create a soft-delete pending action for another administrator’s approval. Verify recipients, delivery locations, and identifiers before submission, and review the resulting action status. Submitting a message to Microsoft helps improve verdict handling, but is not a substitute for removing delivered copies or securing compromised accounts.

sections.title: Interpret AIR accurately
sections.body: Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 AIR examines alerts and related email clusters to establish broader scope. By default its proposed remediation requires SecOps approval. Current MDO automation settings can allow selected malicious cluster types to remediate automatically; clusters larger than 10,000 messages still require review. Avoid the obsolete blanket claim that every AIR action always waits for approval. Review pending actions and completed history, and inspect cluster queries before approving a broad result. Automatic results can appear in EmailPostDeliveryEvents with ActionType Automated Remediation and ActionTrigger Automation.

sections.title: Distinguish removal from containment
sections.body: ZAP retroactively addresses malicious messages delivered to cloud mailboxes; it does not protect an on-premises mailbox in the same way. AIR may still find related mail that earlier cleanup missed. Attack disruption instead targets an active attack using high-confidence correlated signals and can contain users/devices or interrupt identity access, depending on integrated workloads. A disruption banner is a reason to inspect the attack story and actual actions. Deleting phishing copies does not revoke stolen sessions, remove malicious inbox rules, or revoke abusive app consent. Verify those related risks before declaring recovery complete.

remember: MDO AIR remains available after the September 2026 Endpoint AIR change.
MDO AIR defaults to approval, with configurable automatic remediation for eligible clusters.
Propose remediation supports an approval-based soft-delete workflow.
Removal of messages does not by itself recover a compromised identity.
pitfalls: ZAP, AIR, manual removal, and attack disruption are different mechanisms.
Do not infer current location or successful removal solely from the original delivery event.
Restoration depends on retained data and mailbox recovery settings.

lab.title: Review a response decision
steps: In a licensed test tenant, open an existing training investigation or the official AIR walkthrough.
Compare a malicious email cluster with its query scope and latest mailbox count.
Locate pending actions and history; explain who can approve and how you would verify success.
Draft a response checklist covering message removal, sessions, inbox rules, and OAuth grants; execute only against prepared lab assets.
lab.done: Your checklist distinguishes executed cleanup from identity actions still needed.

questions.stem: An organization requires a second administrator to approve analyst-requested deletion of a verified phishing campaign. The analyst is working in Threat Explorer. What should the analyst select?
options: Move or delete immediately, then ask the second administrator to review it later.
Submit to Microsoft only, assuming this removes all copies.
Create a sender allow entry so the messages become easier to identify.
Propose remediation to create a pending soft-delete action.
explanations: Immediate execution does not meet prior-approval requirements.
Submission requests verdict analysis and does not replace tenant cleanup.
Allowing the sender increases risk and does not implement deletion approval.
Correct. Propose remediation supports the two-step approval workflow.
questions.takeaway: Match the response workflow to the required approval boundary.

questions.stem: MDO AIR identifies malicious email clusters. Which TWO statements reflect the current documented approval model?
options: Every malicious cluster always requires approval with no configuration exceptions.
A cluster larger than 10,000 messages is automatically deleted regardless of settings.
Remediation requires approval by default.
Selected cluster types can be configured for automatic remediation, subject to documented limits.
explanations: Current configurable automatic remediation makes this absolute claim wrong.
Large clusters remain pending for review.
Correct. Approval is the default behavior.
Correct. MDO automation settings permit eligible automatic cleanup.
questions.takeaway: Learn the default and its supported exceptions.

questions.stem: ZAP has removed malicious messages from affected cloud mailboxes. Evidence also shows an attacker created a forwarding rule using a stolen session. What must the response include?
options: Disable ZAP because post-delivery removal prevents account investigation.
Investigate and remediate the identity/session and forwarding-rule abuse in addition to confirming mail cleanup.
Only resubmit the original message and wait for a new verdict.
Close the incident because message removal also revokes all sessions and mailbox rules.
explanations: ZAP and identity investigation can work together.
Correct. Account persistence and stolen access are separate response requirements.
Verdict analysis does not revoke the attacker’s access.
ZAP message cleanup does not perform every account-recovery action.
questions.takeaway: Recover the compromised account as well as removing phishing copies.

questions.stem: A BEC incident shows an Attack Disruption tag. An analyst assumes this is just another name for ZAP. Which correction is best?
options: Disruption uses correlated attack evidence to contain compromised assets; ZAP retroactively handles delivered messages.
ZAP disables all on-premises directory accounts involved in any mail incident.
Disruption only changes the subject of suspicious email.
The tag guarantees every persistence mechanism and stolen credential has been remediated.
explanations: Correct. The mechanisms operate at different response scopes.
ZAP is message-oriented and does not universally disable directory accounts.
Disruption can enforce containment and access-related actions.
Containment is not proof of complete eradication and recovery.
questions.takeaway: Identify which control acted and what residual risk remains.

title: Entra identity risk and account recovery
subtitle: Investigate risk at the correct scope and remove attacker access rather than only clearing a flag.
intro: Identity risk is a probability signal that directs investigation and access control. Sign-in risk concerns whether a particular authentication request is legitimate; user risk concerns whether the account is compromised. A user can therefore remain risky after one sign-in issue is resolved. SC-200 scenarios may combine unfamiliar authentication, token theft, leaked credentials, and account actions. Read the risk details and sign-in context before deciding whether the finding is a false positive, an expected risky activity, or a real compromise. Full ID Protection capabilities generally require Entra ID P2 or Entra Suite. Your role and the target user’s administrative status can constrain remediation; a visible report does not guarantee permission to reset or disable an account.

sections.title: Investigate the signal and timeline
sections.body: Review the detected activity, risk state, risk level, IP, device, location, application, authentication details, and Conditional Access result. Compare the event with the user’s normal behavior and other Defender observations. Some detections are calculated offline, so risk can increase after the original authentication. Apparent travel anomalies can reflect network routing, while successful MFA does not universally clear token-theft risk. Correlate request/session identifiers where available and verify the user’s explanation through a trusted channel. Avoid turning a contextual explanation into an automatic dismissal without checking downstream activity.

sections.title: Choose remediation, not cosmetic cleanup
sections.body: For a real compromise, secure credentials and sessions, review authentication methods and app access, and block access when necessary. Confirm user compromised records the finding and elevates risk; it does not itself make the account safe. A password reset is a remediation action, while dismissing risk changes the risk record without changing the password. Current Risky users guidance distinguishes Confirm user safe for false positives from Dismiss user risk for benign positive activity such as an authorized test. Record which situation you established rather than treating those actions as synonyms.

sections.title: Apply risk-based controls correctly
sections.body: Configure current risk-based access policies through Conditional Access: legacy ID Protection risk policies retired October 1, 2026. Sign-in-risk policies can require MFA or reauthentication; user-risk policies can require password change or adaptive risk remediation. A secure password change requires the user to satisfy MFA and differs from recovering an unknown password through SSPR. Hybrid recovery also depends on synchronization and password-writeback design. Test with a limited group and preserve emergency access. Policy enforcement is only one part of recovery when an attacker also changed forwarding rules, registered methods, or granted application access.

remember: Sign-in risk and user risk are different assessment scopes.
Confirm compromised records a finding; subsequent remediation is still required.
Dismissal is not a credential reset.
Use Conditional Access for current risk policies after the October 2026 legacy retirement.
pitfalls: MFA success does not universally negate token-theft detections.
Clearing one risky sign-in does not necessarily clear aggregate user risk.
Confirm safe and dismiss risk have distinct current intended uses.

lab.title: Investigate and plan an identity recovery
steps: In a licensed lab or official ID Protection walkthrough, open a risky-sign-in example and inspect authentication and Conditional Access context.
Compare it with the user-level risk timeline and list which additional evidence affects the decision.
Create a limited-scope report-only risk-based Conditional Access policy where supported.
Write the recovery actions for a real compromise and separately for a verified authorized test; do not dismiss production risk as practice.
lab.done: You can justify the risk scope, correct record action, and credential/session remediation independently.

questions.stem: A user has leaked-credential risk and several suspicious sign-ins. One recent sign-in was legitimate. What is the best next decision?
options: Dismiss all user risk because one sign-in was legitimate.
Treat sign-in risk and user risk as identical fields.
Investigate aggregate user risk and remediate compromised credentials/sessions as supported by evidence.
Remove the user from every risk policy before investigating.
explanations: Other detections still require evaluation.
The two signals have different scope.
Correct. One legitimate event does not settle broader account compromise.
Policy exclusion can restore attacker access without removing the cause.
questions.takeaway: A user-risk investigation must consider all relevant detections.

questions.stem: A stolen-session investigation confirms a real user compromise. Which TWO statements should guide the response?
options: Confirming compromise records the finding but does not by itself secure the account.
Revoking sessions and addressing credentials/authentication methods may be required.
Dismissing risk rotates the user’s password and removes malicious OAuth grants.
A past MFA claim proves the stolen token cannot be abused.
explanations: Correct. The record action is distinct from remediation.
Correct. Recovery must remove the attacker’s access paths.
Dismissal changes risk state and does not perform those recovery actions.
Token-theft detections cannot be dismissed solely because MFA occurred.
questions.takeaway: Mark the true finding and execute the necessary access remediation.

questions.stem: A verified, authorized penetration test produced a real risky activity signal. The account is not compromised, and future similar activity should still be evaluated. Which current Risky users action best matches the intended outcome?
options: Dismiss user risk and document the benign positive activity.
Confirm user safe specifically to reset behavioral learning for a false positive.
Confirm user compromised and stop without remediation.
Reset the password solely to change the alert’s display name.
explanations: Correct. Current guidance uses dismissal for real but nonmalicious risk such as a known test.
Confirm safe is intended for false positives and changes learning behavior.
That records the opposite determination and leaves risk unresolved.
A reset is an account action, not a display-name change.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish benign positive risk from a false-positive detection.

questions.stem: In October 2026 an administrator is replacing a legacy ID Protection user-risk policy. Users must satisfy a current risk-remediation access control. Where should the policy be configured?
options: Purview Content search, because it enforces sign-in grant controls.
Microsoft Entra Conditional Access using a user-risk condition and supported grant control.
An endpoint device group, because user risk is an endpoint automation level.
The retired legacy ID Protection risk-policy page as the long-term configuration.
explanations: Content search retrieves content rather than enforcing authentication policy.
Correct. Current risk policies are configured in Conditional Access.
Device-group automation does not define Entra risk grant controls.
Legacy risk policies retired October 1, 2026.
questions.takeaway: Use the current Conditional Access risk-policy model.

title: Defender for Identity and lateral movement
subtitle: Connect authentication abuse, privileged access, and identity-source-specific response.
intro: A stolen credential can be used across multiple hosts without dropping a new malware file. Defender for Identity supplies identity-centered detections and context for investigating that progression, particularly in hybrid environments. SC-200 expects you to recognize the evidence of reconnaissance, credential theft, privilege escalation, and lateral movement and to choose an appropriate identity response. Do not reduce the investigation to a technique’s name. Establish which account authenticated, where it originated, what resource it reached, and whether that behavior was authorized. Then determine whether the same person or service has linked cloud accounts. Identity-level context can reveal a broader impact than one alert, but actions still depend on the system that actually manages each account.

sections.title: Read authentication in context
sections.body: Open the identity alert and its affected assets, then review the chronological evidence available in that alert format. Defender for Identity alerts currently have classic and unified Defender layouts, so a particular alert-story panel may be absent without the underlying detection being missing. Suspected pass-the-ticket, suspicious directory enumeration, or replication-related activity should prompt examination of source, target, account privilege, protocol, and timing. Legitimate administration can resemble malicious behavior. Compare change records and known management hosts, and expand to linked endpoint activity before deciding the event is expected.

sections.title: Investigate routes and actual movement
sections.body: Identity pages consolidate related accounts, observed activity, alerts, and exposure. Attack-path information helps identify potential routes toward sensitive resources. A potential route is not proof that the attacker traversed it; verify actual sign-ins, endpoint events, and directory changes. For a lateral-movement hypothesis, reconstruct the source-to-target chain and determine whether privileged credentials were exposed along it. Reduce ongoing access and examine other hosts reached by the same identity. Track related accounts carefully so that disabling a cloud account does not leave an abused on-premises account active.

sections.title: Respond through the account’s authority
sections.body: Supported identity actions include disabling accounts, revoking sessions for supported providers, and forcing a password change where supported. Availability varies by connected identity source and role; not every provider supports every action. Current Defender for Identity guidance executes Active Directory remediation through a sensor on a domain controller. Sensors on AD FS, AD CS, or Entra Connect servers do not perform those directory actions. Sensor v3.x uses the domain controller’s LocalSystem account, so old gMSA-only instructions are insufficient for v3 deployments. Verify prerequisites and Action center results, then separately address persistence and any exposed privileged access.

remember: Potential attack paths describe exposure; observed events establish actual movement.
Classic and unified identity alerts can present the same detection family differently.
Identity response actions depend on account source and analyst authorization.
Sensor v3.x uses the domain controller LocalSystem account for remediation.
pitfalls: Disabling one linked account does not automatically prove every account is secured.
An alert on a familiar admin tool is not automatically a false positive.
Endpoint user containment and directory-account disable have different enforcement scope.

lab.title: Trace an identity movement scenario
steps: Use the official alert documentation and a lab incident with identity evidence.
Identify source host, target host, account, protocol, privilege, and event times.
Open the identity page and compare a potential attack path with observed activity.
Check your lab sensor version, action-account configuration, and permissions; document how you would verify an account-disable action.
lab.done: You can distinguish potential exposure, observed movement, and the system that executes account remediation.

sources.title: Classic alert layouts and lateral movement

questions.stem: A pass-the-ticket alert involves a service account and two servers. The account owner says the service is business critical. What should the analyst establish before choosing a proportionate response?
options: That a business-critical account can never be contained or disabled.
That any use of Kerberos is malicious.
Source/target authentication context, account privilege, authorization, and related activity.
Only whether the account’s display name contains the word service.
explanations: Criticality influences response planning but does not justify leaving active compromise unchecked.
Kerberos is a normal authentication protocol; abuse requires evidence.
Correct. These details establish behavior, scope, and operational impact.
A naming convention does not establish authorization.
questions.takeaway: Investigate identity behavior and business impact together.

questions.stem: An identity page shows a possible route from a workstation user to a critical server. Which TWO conclusions or actions are valid?
options: Close the identity alert because attack paths contain no useful investigative context.
Treat the path as exposure information requiring validation against actual events.
Examine observed account and device activity to determine whether the route was used.
Declare that every path edge is a completed malicious authentication.
explanations: Exposure context helps prioritize validation and containment.
Correct. Potential reachability is not an observed compromise.
Correct. Event evidence tests the movement hypothesis.
Path relationships do not prove traversal.
questions.takeaway: Separate the possible blast radius from the proven attack sequence.

questions.stem: A mixed sensor deployment includes Defender for Identity sensor v3.x. An old runbook requires a gMSA action account for all Active Directory remediation. Which correction is needed?
options: Use the documented LocalSystem model for v3.x and validate the mixed-deployment setting.
Force v3.x to use the old gMSA action account.
Assume a Security Reader can perform every account-disable action.
Run Active Directory remediation through an AD FS-only sensor.
explanations: Correct. V3.x always uses the domain controller LocalSystem account for these actions.
V3.x does not use gMSA action accounts.
Read access does not grant all response permissions.
These actions execute through domain-controller sensors.
questions.takeaway: Check sensor-version-specific action prerequisites.

questions.stem: An analyst sees linked Active Directory and Entra accounts for a compromised identity. The desired response is to interrupt access across affected accounts. What is the best approach?
options: Delete the identity profile to guarantee that all documents and accounts are removed.
Assume every connected SaaS provider supports identical session-revocation actions.
Choose supported actions for the relevant accounts/sources and verify each result in Action center.
Disable only the Entra account and assume the on-premises account is disabled by definition.
explanations: Profile deletion is not the documented containment workflow.
Supported actions vary by identity source.
Correct. The account authority and connector determine action execution.
Linked identity context does not make all account states identical.
questions.takeaway: Apply and verify remediation at the actual account authority.

title: Cloud Apps, OAuth abuse, and SaaS governance
subtitle: Investigate activity context and app grants, then verify connector-specific remediation.
intro: Cloud abuse can involve stolen user sessions, excessive file access, public sharing, or an OAuth app that received permission to read data. Resetting a user’s password may leave an abusive application grant intact. Defender for Cloud Apps supplies activity context, app governance, and supported governance actions for connected services. SC-200 scenarios require distinguishing a risky user action from an application-permission problem and matching the response to the affected object. A country anomaly, high permission, or unfamiliar publisher increases concern but needs contextual investigation. Your conclusion should identify who or what accessed data, what authorization permitted it, and what action actually removed that access. Connector support and policy transitions constrain the available tools.

sections.title: Investigate the activity
sections.body: Review the alert’s account, application, IP, location, activity sequence, and surrounding access pattern. Check known corporate egress, VPN use, travel, and authorized bulk operations before deciding an anomaly is malicious. Look for corroboration such as new consent, unusual downloads, unexpected sharing, or other identity risk. Current anomaly detections have been transitioning toward dynamic threat detection; learn the investigative questions rather than memorizing one historical policy-menu layout. Establish the time window and affected objects so that remediation targets the actual exposure rather than every user who touched the application.

sections.title: Treat OAuth grants as an access path
sections.body: App governance provides visibility into OAuth-enabled apps and their permission usage. Investigate requested permissions against the app’s business purpose, publisher, user population, consent timing, and related activity. A rarely used utility with broad mailbox access deserves attention, but low popularity alone is not proof. Inspect consent and activity evidence to determine affected users and data. For a confirmed abusive app, use supported ban/revoke or governance controls and remove the inappropriate grants. Also investigate compromised users and sessions; revoking an app and resetting a password address different access mechanisms.

sections.title: Select and verify governance
sections.body: Governance actions depend on the connector and object: user/session actions differ from file sharing, quarantine, or trash actions. Review the Governance log for success or failure and supported retry/revert behavior. Quarantine restoration can change sharing or version behavior, so plan recovery with the app owner. As researched October 15, 2026, Microsoft schedules Cloud Apps file-policy retirement for January 6, 2027 and recommends migration to Purview DLP or auto-labeling. Learn the current file-governance concepts for the exam while checking the tenant’s feature status. An alert alone does not prove the associated policy action completed.

remember: A password reset and revocation of an abusive OAuth grant address different risks.
Compare permissions with business purpose and observed usage.
Governance actions vary by connected service and object type.
File-policy retirement is scheduled for January 6, 2027; verify current tenant availability.
pitfalls: An anomaly needs corroboration; VPN routing can explain location changes.
Cloud app discovery or a risk label alone is not proof of enforced blocking.
Do not assume an alert guarantees successful governance execution.

lab.title: Inspect a test app and governance trail
steps: Open Cloud Apps app governance in a properly licensed test tenant.
Review a known benign test application’s permissions, consenting users, publisher, and recent activity.
Choose a prepared test object and inspect which governance actions the connector actually supports.
If you execute an approved reversible lab action, verify the Governance log and restore the object according to its documented semantics.
lab.done: You can explain an app’s access and distinguish a policy match from a successfully enforced action.

questions.stem: A cloud activity alert shows geographically distant access within minutes. The organization uses several VPN exits. What is the best first investigative step?
options: Disable every user who signed in from either country.
Treat geography alone as proof that files were exfiltrated.
Dismiss it solely because the organization owns a VPN.
Correlate IP ownership, known VPN egress, user activity, and other compromise indicators.
explanations: This response is not proportionate to the current evidence.
Location alone does not establish data access or theft.
The VPN explanation must match the actual observations.
Correct. Network and behavioral context test the anomaly.
questions.takeaway: Validate anomalies with environmental and behavioral context.

questions.stem: A newly consented application has broad mail access and activity inconsistent with its stated purpose. Which TWO steps directly address the investigation and response?
options: Reset one user’s password and assume all app permissions are removed.
Declare the app safe because a user accepted the consent screen.
Review consent, permissions, affected users, and related app activity.
If confirmed abusive, revoke/ban it through supported controls and address inappropriate grants.
explanations: A password reset does not universally revoke application grants.
Consent can be socially engineered or overly broad.
Correct. These establish authorization and actual impact.
Correct. App-based access must be removed through its supported governance path.
questions.takeaway: Investigate and remove the application access path itself.

questions.stem: A policy matched a sensitive shared file, but the owner says external collaborators still have access. What should be checked before declaring remediation successful?
options: The connector-supported governance action and its result in Governance log.
The number of other cloud applications in the discovery catalog.
Only whether the file’s name contains the word confidential.
Only whether the policy generated an alert.
explanations: Correct. Support and execution state establish whether access changed.
Catalog size does not report this action’s outcome.
File naming does not prove access control.
Detection does not guarantee enforcement.
questions.takeaway: Verify the actual governance result on the affected object.

questions.stem: In October 2026 a team is designing long-term file-data protection around Cloud Apps file policies. What documented lifecycle change should influence the design?
options: Plan migration to Purview DLP or auto-labeling because file policies are scheduled to retire January 6, 2027.
Assume the retirement date proves current alerts contain no useful evidence.
Assume every Cloud Apps capability retires on that date.
Replace OAuth governance with endpoint antivirus exclusions.
explanations: Correct. The notice specifically concerns file policies and identifies replacement approaches.
Current evidence remains investigable regardless of a future policy transition.
The notice does not retire the entire service.
Antivirus exclusions do not replace SaaS permission governance.
questions.takeaway: Separate current investigation skills from a feature’s future lifecycle.

title: Defender for Cloud workload incidents
subtitle: Identify the affected resource and protection plan, then respond to workload-specific evidence.
intro: Cloud response begins by identifying the resource and activity, not by applying a workstation action to everything in the subscription. A suspicious container process, a malicious blob, a server alert, and an unusual resource-management operation need different evidence and remediation. Defender for Cloud combines workload threat protection with posture information, but a recommendation about a weakness is different from an alert about observed activity. SC-200 expects you to investigate workload alerts and connect them to the wider incident. Verify that the relevant protection plan and supporting components cover the resource, establish the activity’s scope, and involve the workload owner when containment could interrupt production or destroy evidence.

sections.title: Read the alert and plan coverage
sections.body: Review resource identifiers, activity time, affected assets, detection details, IPs, processes, and any recommended investigation steps. A security alert’s status is a workflow field; changing it does not apply the recommended resource fix. Match protection to the resource: Servers for machines, Containers for Kubernetes, Storage for storage threats, Databases for database activity, and the relevant App Service, Key Vault, Resource Manager, API, or AI protection capability for those surfaces. Foundational posture coverage does not imply that every paid workload detection is enabled. Check actual scope and multicloud support instead of assuming identical capabilities everywhere.

sections.title: Choose server and container evidence
sections.body: Defender for Servers Plan 1 emphasizes endpoint detection and response integration; Plan 2 adds capabilities such as agentless scanning, file integrity monitoring, and just-in-time access. Do not confuse a patch recommendation with a completed server compromise. For Kubernetes, distinguish control-plane API operations from runtime activity in workloads. Validate namespace, pod, container image digest, service account, and source identity, then inspect related cluster events. Deleting one pod may not remove a malicious deployment controller or stolen credentials. Supported detections depend on Kubernetes distribution and installed Defender components.

sections.title: Handle malicious storage safely
sections.body: Defender for Storage malware scanning can expose results through blob index tags, Defender alerts for malicious files, and optionally Event Grid or Log Analytics. Choose the signal and response channel that matches latency and auditing requirements. Event-driven automation can quarantine or move content, and current built-in malicious-blob soft deletion is another supported option when configured. Preserve evidence and prevent unsafe downstream processing; do not assume a tag alone enforces an access boundary. After remediation, verify both the object state and the access path, and investigate whether compromised identities or other resources were involved.

remember: Recommendations describe posture; alerts describe detected suspicious activity.
Verify workload plan, scope, connector, and component coverage.
Container control-plane and runtime evidence answer different questions.
A scan-result signal needs configured enforcement to change object access.
pitfalls: Closing an alert is not the same as changing the resource.
Removing a pod may leave the deployment or access credentials intact.
A paid plan on one resource type does not enable all other workload plans.

lab.title: Triage a workload alert
steps: Use official sample alerts or a nonproduction Defender for Cloud environment.
Open an alert and list the resource ID, activity, identity, evidence, and applicable workload plan.
For a container example, identify control-plane versus runtime evidence and the owning deployment.
For a storage example, map the scan result to a configured response and explain how you would verify object state.
lab.done: Your response plan names the actual resource, evidence source, containment owner, and success check.

sources.title: Manage and respond to cloud alerts

questions.stem: A cloud workload alert includes a resource ID, suspicious source IP, and recommended remediation. An analyst changes its status without changing the resource. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Only the alert workflow state changed; resource remediation still requires execution and verification.
The source IP is now blocked on all subscriptions.
Changing status automatically applies every recommendation.
The affected resource was deleted as a side effect.
explanations: Correct. Alert management and resource response are different actions.
A status change does not create a global network block.
Recommendations require the appropriate actual response.
Deletion is not implied by workflow status.
questions.takeaway: Verify the resource action instead of relying on alert closure.

questions.stem: A suspicious Kubernetes event may involve a malicious deployment. Which TWO checks best support a complete investigation?
options: Assume every cluster distribution produces identical detections without component prerequisites.
Assume deleting one pod guarantees the deployment cannot recreate it.
Determine whether the evidence concerns API control-plane activity or workload runtime behavior.
Identify the workload owner/controller, namespace, image, and service account before deciding remediation scope.
explanations: Distribution and component coverage affect supported detection.
A controller can recreate a deleted pod.
Correct. The evidence surface determines the investigative path.
Correct. These identifiers support scope and durable remediation.
questions.takeaway: Investigate the Kubernetes control and execution surfaces separately.

questions.stem: A storage processing pipeline must react quickly when a malware scan completes. The team also needs a separate queryable audit trail. Which design best fits?
options: Use configured Event Grid delivery for response automation and Log Analytics for centralized analysis.
Read only an alert’s severity once per month and treat it as immediate enforcement.
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 1 as the blob malware response mechanism.
Assume a blob index tag automatically blocks all reads without any access policy.
explanations: Correct. These channels serve event-driven response and log analysis respectively.
Monthly review does not satisfy rapid response.
Server EDR is not the storage scanning response channel.
Tags are signals; enforcement requires a configured control.
questions.takeaway: Choose delivery and enforcement mechanisms that match latency and audit requirements.

questions.stem: A team needs server EDR plus file integrity monitoring and just-in-time VM access through Defender for Cloud. Which plan satisfies this stated combination?
options: Defender for Servers Plan 2, with required features configured.
Defender for Storage alone because all paid plans provide identical server features.
Foundational CSPM alone with no workload protection plan.
Defender for Servers Plan 1 alone because it includes every Plan 2 feature.
explanations: Correct. Plan 2 adds these capabilities beyond the Plan 1 EDR focus.
Storage and server plans protect different workloads.
Foundational posture management does not supply these paid server protections.
Plan 1 does not provide the full stated Plan 2 combination.
questions.takeaway: Match the requested capabilities to the correct workload plan and settings.

title: Purview investigations and Microsoft Graph activity
subtitle: Choose activity records, content search, or API telemetry according to the question being asked.
intro: “Who did it?”, “What content is involved?”, and “Which API requests were made?” require different evidence. Purview Audit records supported user and administrator activities. Content search in eDiscovery finds matching mailbox and site content. Microsoft Graph activity logs describe requests processed by Graph and can expose application or user API abuse. SC-200 explicitly includes all three investigative approaches, plus response to Purview-identified threats. A strong analyst selects the evidence source before writing a query, then verifies collection, access, retention, and timing. These tools complement each other: finding a document does not prove it was downloaded, and a successful API request does not by itself explain every item returned.

sections.title: Use Audit for activity
sections.body: Search Purview Audit by the relevant UTC interval, users, workload, and operation, then inspect record details such as actor, object, and result. Verify that auditing and required permissions were in place. Audit Standard generally retains records for 180 days; eligible Audit Premium licensing provides a one-year default for specified workloads, with retention policies and user licensing affecting availability. A broad search can take time, and records are not guaranteed to appear immediately. An empty result therefore requires checking scope, collection, licensing, retention, and ingestion delay before concluding that no activity occurred.

sections.title: Use eDiscovery for content
sections.body: Content search now lives inside the eDiscovery experience and its Content Search case. Scope mailbox/site data sources and use the supported KeyQL conditions to find relevant items. KeyQL content properties differ from the KQL event queries used in Defender and Sentinel. Review estimates and sampled results, refine the search, and preserve or export content using the appropriate authorized workflow. A search alone does not establish a preservation hold. Cases organize searches, holds, and review work; premium features and data access depend on subscription and permissions. Do not use a content match as proof of a user action.

sections.title: Use Graph logs for API behavior
sections.body: Enable Microsoft Graph activity-log collection through Entra diagnostic settings with the required P1/P2 tenant license, Azure destination, and setup permissions. In Log Analytics, MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs includes request URI/method, response code, app/service-principal/user IDs, IP, and sign-in correlation fields. Examine a suspicious app’s sequence and distinguish denied requests from successful ones. These logs do not backfill uncollected history or expose an app’s activity in another resource tenant. Correlate with sign-ins and consent/directory audit records to understand who authorized access.
sections.code:
MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResponseStatusCode == 403
| summarize DeniedRequests=count() by AppId, RequestMethod, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

sections.title: Understand Purview signals in Defender
sections.body: DLP evidence can connect sensitive-data activity to users, files, and devices, with supported remediation such as unsharing a file. As of early October 2026, Microsoft documents a built-in tuning change that represents DLP signals as behaviors in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities rather than alerts by default. Disable that tuning rule if the organization needs the documented DLP alert/incident workflow. Validate permissions before inspecting sensitive content, then confirm whether the selected action changed access. A missing DLP incident is not sufficient evidence that no DLP signal exists.

remember: Audit searches activities; eDiscovery searches content; Graph activity logs show API requests.
KeyQL for content search is distinct from KQL for telemetry.
Check retention and collection before interpreting empty results.
Current DLP tuning can route signals to behavior tables rather than incident alerts.
pitfalls: A search is not a preservation hold.
A 403 response is a denied request, not proof of successful exfiltration.
The Graph auditLogs API and Graph activity logs are related but different data concepts.

lab.title: Compare three evidence sources
steps: Search a harmless known lab action in Purview Audit using UTC and the specific operation.
Create an eDiscovery content search for a known test message or file, scoped to its data source.
Where Graph logging is enabled, run the example denied-request query and inspect an individual event.
Explain which source answers actor activity, item content, and API behavior; note each visibility limit.
lab.done: You can select the correct source and interpret its result without making unsupported cross-source assumptions.

sources.title: eDiscovery components and Content Search case

questions.stem: An investigator must determine who shared a file externally and separately retrieve the relevant document for review. Which pairing is appropriate?
options: Purview Audit for the sharing activity, then eDiscovery content search for the document.
Graph request volume alone as the full document-content archive.
eDiscovery content search alone as proof of the sharing actor and operation.
Device antivirus history for the document’s external sharing permissions.
explanations: Correct. Activity records and content retrieval answer different investigative questions.
API request metadata is not a document archive.
Finding content does not prove the sharing action.
Antivirus history does not replace SaaS sharing audit evidence.
questions.takeaway: Choose evidence by question: activity versus content.

questions.stem: A suspicious application makes Graph calls. Which TWO fields or checks directly help determine what requests were made and whether access succeeded?
options: RequestUri and RequestMethod.
ResponseStatusCode, correlated with app/user and sign-in context.
The display name of an unrelated Sentinel workbook.
A content-search estimate treated as the HTTP response body for every Graph call.
explanations: Correct. These identify API target and operation.
Correct. Status and identity context support outcome analysis.
Workbook naming does not describe the app’s requests.
Content-search estimates are not Graph response payloads.
questions.takeaway: Inspect actual Graph request metadata and status before claiming access.

questions.stem: A lab query returns many Graph requests with ResponseStatusCode 403. What does the result establish?
options: No further evidence is needed because every denied request is automatically benign.
All those requests successfully extracted the requested files.
Those observed requests were denied; investigate their target, identity, and surrounding successful calls.
The service principal never authenticated anywhere.
explanations: Repeated denied enumeration or privilege probes can be suspicious.
403 indicates forbidden access rather than successful extraction.
Correct. Denial is an outcome that still merits context.
Denied API access does not prove absence of authentication.
questions.takeaway: A failed attempt and successful impact are different findings.

questions.stem: In October 2026 a team stops seeing DLP incidents, although relevant signals remain in advanced hunting. What current documented behavior should it check first?
options: Whether the endpoint was isolated, because isolation clears historical compliance evidence.
Whether all eDiscovery cases were deleted, because cases are required to ingest every DLP signal.
Whether a 403 Graph event automatically suppresses all DLP alerts tenant-wide.
The built-in DLP alert-tuning rule that represents signals as behaviors in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities.
explanations: Endpoint isolation does not erase the historical signal model.
eDiscovery cases are not a universal DLP-ingestion prerequisite.
A denied Graph request does not create this global behavior.
Correct. The early-October tuning change directly explains this symptom.
questions.takeaway: Check signal representation and tuning before declaring a detection gap.

title: Security Copilot and agentic investigation
subtitle: Use AI summaries and agents to accelerate work while verifying evidence, permissions, and results.
intro: Security Copilot can help an analyst interpret an attack story, summarize entities, explain scripts, and identify response steps. Agentic capabilities can perform supported tasks across multiple reasoning and tool steps. SC-200 now explicitly expects familiarity with these investigation experiences. The critical skill is choosing the capability that addresses the bottleneck while preserving evidence-based judgment. A summary can accelerate orientation, but it is not an independent telemetry source or a guarantee that every affected asset has been found. A deployed agent’s action scope depends on its identity, permissions, configured triggers, licensing, and available data. Review both what the AI concludes and what tools or actions actually executed before relying on the result.

sections.title: Use embedded assistance for a specific question
sections.body: Within Defender, incident summarization helps orient you to affected entities and the timeline. Guided responses suggest triage, containment, investigation, or remediation steps with contextual reasons. Script analysis can explain suspicious command lines and associated techniques from incident or timeline context. Ask precise questions that identify the incident, time window, or entity. If a summary omits an important alert or the script explanation conflicts with observed execution, inspect the source evidence and refine the question. Useful AI output should help you make a better-supported next decision, not merely restate an alert title.

sections.title: Distinguish an agent from a prompt
sections.body: Agents can run triggered workflows with defined identities and action rights. The Phishing Triage Agent processes supported user-reported phishing alerts, provides a classification rationale, and leaves true-positive incidents for further analyst response. The Security Alert Triage Agent extends that model to additional workloads in preview; current availability and prerequisites vary by alert type. The Security Store also exposes other agents for threat intelligence, hunting, and analysis. Do not assume every tenant has the same preview capability or that deploying an agent grants unrestricted access to every data source.

sections.title: Review reasoning and operational boundaries
sections.body: Check the agent’s activity, verdict rationale, tools, and observable outcomes. A workflow graph can show its steps; feedback helps adapt supported behavior, but human feedback itself requires governance because a mistaken lesson can influence future classifications. Security Copilot access and underlying workload permissions remain relevant, as do capacity and plugin availability. An AI recommendation to isolate a device does not mean the action executed successfully. Preserve the investigation record, validate any generated query before acting on its results, and distinguish a proposed step from a completed action in the Action center or workload history.

remember: Summarization, script analysis, guided response, and triggered agents serve different tasks.
Agent identity, triggers, permissions, and workload prerequisites define its scope.
Verify generated explanations against source events.
A recommendation is distinct from an executed response action.
pitfalls: Fluent wording does not prove a correct conclusion.
Preview agent capabilities and supported alert types can vary by tenant.
A true-positive triage verdict is not proof of full remediation.

lab.title: Evaluate AI-assisted investigation
steps: With provisioned access, open a lab incident and request a summary with the affected entities and timeline.
Compare each material statement with the underlying alert evidence.
Analyze a harmless prepared script or command line and identify any unsupported assumptions in the explanation.
Review an available agent’s trigger, identity, permissions, and activity trace; document where analyst follow-up remains necessary.
lab.done: You can substantiate the AI output and identify exactly which actions were proposed versus completed.

questions.stem: A known endpoint event contains an obfuscated command line. Arrange a workflow that uses Copilot to explain it while reaching an evidence-based response decision.
options: Read the analysis, inspect the displayed code, and review associated techniques.
Validate the explanation against execution context and choose the justified investigative or response step.
Locate the exact script/command-line event in the incident attack story or device timeline.
Select Analyze to request script analysis in the Copilot pane.
explanations: Review the generated interpretation after analysis is available.
Validation and the response decision follow the generated explanation.
First identify the exact event so analysis has the intended evidence context.
Start analysis only after selecting the relevant event.
questions.takeaway: Use script analysis to inform an evidence-based decision, then verify the result.

questions.stem: Before relying on an agent’s autonomous triage, which TWO checks are essential?
options: Assume the agent can access every workload regardless of license.
Treat every recommended containment action as already completed successfully.
Review its rationale and activity trace against available evidence.
Verify its configured identity, permissions, triggers, and supported alert types.
explanations: Licensing and workload access still apply.
Recommendations and completed operations are distinct.
Correct. Evidence and traceability support trustworthy conclusions.
Correct. These define what the agent can see and do.
questions.takeaway: Understand scope and verify evidence before accepting automated conclusions.

questions.stem: The Phishing Triage Agent classifies a reported message as a true positive. The incident remains open and in progress. What should the analyst infer?
options: The message must be a false positive because open status contradicts its verdict.
The threat needs further analyst investigation and response; true-positive triage does not imply completed recovery.
The agent failed because every true positive must be automatically closed.
Every affected account and device has already been recovered.
explanations: Classification and workflow status answer different questions.
Correct. The documented workflow leaves malicious findings for analyst follow-up.
An open true-positive incident is expected behavior.
Triage does not prove comprehensive recovery.
questions.takeaway: Use the triage verdict to prioritize the remaining response.

questions.stem: A manager asks why the Security Alert Triage Agent is available in one tenant while another shows only the Phishing Triage Agent. What is the best current explanation?
options: The tenant without the expanded agent cannot investigate phishing manually.
Every tenant must show identical agents because the names are cosmetic.
Installing an unrelated email connector automatically grants every preview and license.
The expanded agent has preview eligibility and workload-specific prerequisites; availability is tenant dependent.
explanations: Manual investigation remains available with appropriate licensing and access.
Availability is not universally identical.
Connector installation does not grant all preview capabilities.
Correct. Current documentation explicitly distinguishes preview access and supported workloads.
questions.takeaway: Read current agent prerequisites instead of assuming universal feature parity.

title: Sentinel incident investigation and case management
subtitle: Coordinate evidence, ownership, tasks, and closure across the unified response workflow.
intro: An investigation can be technically sound and still fail operationally if no one owns the remaining actions. Case management organizes incident context, evidence, tasks, collaboration, and a record of decisions. Sentinel contributes alerts and investigative data, while the Defender portal provides a unified experience when the workspace is onboarded. SC-200 includes response to Sentinel-identified incidents and case management, so prepare for both investigative decisions and workflow requirements. As researched October 15, 2026, incident cases are a recommended preview experience and legacy incidents remain available. Generic cases track other SOC work. Read the scenario’s portal and case type before applying assumptions about status, permissions, task behavior, or closure.

sections.title: Investigate the Sentinel contribution
sections.body: For a Sentinel alert, inspect the analytic rule, mapped entities, triggering events, and time range. The incident’s relationship view is more useful when entity mappings identify accounts, hosts, and IPs consistently. Pivot into raw logs to verify the detection, then examine related activity and other incidents to expand scope. In the legacy Azure experience, bookmarks can preserve a relevant query/result with notes and mapped entities, and the incident timeline can include alerts and bookmarks. A bookmark without entity mapping cannot support the same graph investigation. Portal-specific bookmark creation and action support can differ.

sections.title: Manage accountable work
sections.body: Assign the case owner and create tasks with clear actions, assignees, due dates, and closing notes. The owner coordinates the case; task ownership identifies who performs an individual step. Comments and activity history record investigation decisions and automated changes. Templates can standardize custom fields, statuses, and SLA policies so that a critical incident captures required business context. Do not mark a containment task complete simply because someone assigned it. Verify the actual response action, record evidence of success or failure, and update the task outcome for the next shift.

sections.title: Close or merge with evidence
sections.body: Related incident cases can be merged when shared evidence shows they belong in one investigation and the analyst has access and management permission for all involved cases. Current preview guidance excludes resolved cases from manual merge. At closure, document classification, determination when available, and recovery notes. In current incident cases, closing/resolving the case syncs the related incident state, but related alerts retain their own status and are not automatically resolved. This differs from assumptions built around older experiences. Confirm alert and case state as required by the workflow, and keep residual remediation in an owned task or follow-up case.

remember: Case ownership and individual task ownership serve different coordination needs.
Current incident cases are preview; legacy portal behavior can differ.
Case closure does not automatically resolve related alerts in the current case experience.
Merge requires appropriate management access to all involved cases.
pitfalls: A saved query/result is evidence context, not a remediation action.
A task’s completion must reflect an observed result.
Do not apply Azure legacy instructions blindly to Defender incident cases.

lab.title: Run a documented handoff
steps: Open a lab Sentinel incident or current incident case and inspect the raw events behind one alert.
Record the affected entities, detection logic, and a justified next step.
Create or outline two tasks with separate owners, success criteria, and due dates.
Prepare closing notes that distinguish case status, alert status, containment results, and remaining work.
lab.done: Another analyst can reproduce the finding and identify ownership of every remaining action.

sources.title: Manage incident cases and closure behavior
Sentinel incident raw events and timeline

questions.stem: A SOC needs to require business-service information and apply consistent response due-date policies to incident cases. Which approach best supports that requirement?
options: Disable incident ownership so every analyst receives the same implicit assignment.
Rename the Log Analytics workspace for each new incident.
Configure the supported case template’s custom fields and SLA policies.
Put the service name only in a private analyst note and use no shared workflow.
explanations: Removing ownership weakens accountability.
Workspace naming is not a case-template mechanism.
Correct. Templates standardize required case data and SLA behavior.
Private notes do not enforce shared required fields or SLAs.
questions.takeaway: Use case templates for standardized operational requirements.

questions.stem: A case is handed to another shift while an endpoint action is pending. Which TWO practices best preserve accountability?
options: Mark the task closed because the action was requested.
Document the pending action, success criterion, and current evidence in shared task/case records.
Delete action history so the next shift starts without distracting context.
Keep the case owner and individual response-task assignee explicit.
explanations: Requested does not mean executed successfully.
Correct. Shared state makes the next action verifiable.
History is important for continuity and auditability.
Correct. Coordination ownership and execution ownership both matter.
questions.takeaway: Track who acts, what remains, and how success will be checked.

questions.stem: An analyst resolves a current preview incident case in the Defender portal. Some related alerts remain open. What is the documented interpretation?
options: It is impossible because every case closure always resolves every alert.
This can be expected: case closure syncs the incident state, while related alerts retain their own status.
The alerts must have been deleted and recreated by an attacker.
The case can never be closed unless the workspace is removed from Defender.
explanations: That assumes different workflow behavior than the current case model.
Correct. The current incident-case documentation explicitly describes this behavior.
Open alerts do not imply attacker manipulation of workflow records.
Workspace removal is not a closure prerequisite.
questions.takeaway: Use the current case model’s separate alert-state semantics.

questions.stem: Two unresolved incident cases represent the same attack. The analyst has the required access. Arrange an evidence-based manual merge workflow.
options: Review the combined case and confirm that relevant context is retained.
Confirm the shared attack evidence and that both cases are eligible.
Enter the documented reason/comment and submit the merge.
Select the related cases and open Merge cases.
explanations: Review retained context after the operation completes.
First verify both the investigative reason and current merge constraints.
Document why the cases belong together before executing the merge.
Selection follows the eligibility and relationship check.
questions.takeaway: Case consolidation requires eligibility, an evidence-based reason, and post-merge verification.
